title: "07 · Street geometry and orientation"
execute:
  enabled: false
---

What the shape of a street network says about the place, measured three ways
over three neighborhoods. Orientation entropy separates them cleanly:
L'Eixample in València, a nineteenth-century grid, scores 2.76 nats with 16 % of
its streets in a single sector, while the Albaicín in Granada scores 3.50,
within 2 % of the theoretical maximum, which is another way of saying it has no
dominant direction at all. Circuity agrees, 1.015 against 1.094.

One figure is deliberately not drawn. Coloring streets by bearing is impossible
here: an edge attribute is averaged onto the vertices, bearing is circular, and
at 95 % of the intersections where two orientations meet the average is more
than 5° from every street that touches it. The map would show a direction that
does not exist in the data, so the distribution and the rose carry that material
instead.
